name: PIQA
description: Physical Interaction: Question Answering (PIQA) is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. Given a physical goal and two possible solutions, a model or human must choose the most appropriate solution, of which exactly one is correct.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
citeAs: Bisk, Yonatan; Zellers, Rowan; Le Bras, Ronan; Gao, Jianfeng; Choi, Yejin. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. 2020.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected as goal-solution pairs for multiple-choice question answering. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com and asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable, then construct a physical goal, a valid solution, and a permutation of their own solution that makes it invalid. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Additional HITs were run for qualification prior to the main annotation stage and validation afterwards. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data, Web Scraping
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The annotation prompts were derived from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair, where users provide instructions and often images or videos detailing each step and a list of required tools.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm. AFLite discards instances whose feature representations are highly indicative of the target label. In practice, the authors used 5,000 examples from the original dataset to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of remaining instances; an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data was then used to identify and remove biased or trivial examples. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Examples with low agreement were removed during validation. This often removed correct examples that required expert-level domain knowledge. The interface included a diff button highlighting where the two solutions differ to improve annotator accuracy and speed. Goals were tokenized by Spacy for analysis, and the paper notes all data was collected in English.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked to construct two-component tasks inspired by instructables: articulate a physical goal, write a valid solution, and provide a trick or permutation of their own solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT required annotators to identify well-constructed versus underspecified goal-solution pairs with greater than 80% accuracy to participate in the main HIT. Validation was performed by other annotators for correctness, and examples with low agreement were removed. Human evaluation used majority vote, and annotators for that evaluation were chosen from workers who achieved at least 90% on the qualification HIT.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. The paper notes that some development-set 'mistakes' were actually correct but required a web search to verify. The authors also discuss that annotators were free to create subtle deceptions, including one-word differences, negation, numerical changes, or swapping a key action or item for a topically similar but unhelpful one.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotator self-reporting on turkerview.com was mentioned for pay estimation.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that modeling physical commonsense knowledge is critical for day-to-day human life and important for AI systems and robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors aim for PIQA to provide insight and a benchmark for progress toward language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, enabling language models useful beyond the NLP community.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly discusses reporting bias as a challenge in physical commonsense text data: facts about everyday physical commonsense are rarely directly reported. In early unconstrained prompting, reporting bias swamped the dataset, with annotators drawn to prototypical solutions and common kitchen or garage tools rather than the broader range of everyday objects. The authors addressed this by prompting with instructables to flatten the distribution of referenced objects and by using AFLite to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that text is inherently limited in physical domains due to reporting bias and argues that learning about the world from language alone is limiting. Some examples removed during validation required expert-level knowledge and were considered outside commonsense. The authors also note that automated methods trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance, and that future systems might match humans by finding large in-domain data and fine-tuning heavily, but that this is not the intended point of the benchmark.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is introduced as a benchmark for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models. It is used with train, development, and test splits for benchmarking multiple-choice question answering systems and for diagnostic analysis of model errors and physical commonsense knowledge gaps.
